text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with an unusual payoff structure — each token kept privately earns 1 point but costs every other member 0.75 points, while contributions to the group account yield a 0.75 multiplier benefit for everyone. I'm working out the full payoff formula for member i based on their own kept tokens and the total group contribution.

Calculating out the incentives: keeping a token nets me +1 but costs others 2.25 total, while contributing nets me only 0.75 but has no negative externality — so socially contributing is better (net +0.75 vs net -1.25), yet individually keeping dominates since 1 > 0.75. That makes full defection (keeping everything) the Nash equilibrium, yielding only 20 points each, versus full cooperation yielding 105 points each — a classic social dilemma where individual rationality undermines collective welfare.

Without knowing others' strategies, I can't tit-for-tat, but I could signal cooperative intent early and see how the group responds. I'll settle on contributing a moderate amount, around 10, as a probe to test reciprocity without risking too much.
